title: Absorption by Roots
tagline: Imbibition, diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis and root pressure — how water and minerals enter the root hair.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Water enters a plant entirely through the roots, and the mechanism is physical before it is biological. This chapter builds the three processes in order — imbibition (adsorption of water by solids), diffusion (net movement down a concentration gradient) and osmosis (diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane) — then shows how the root hair cell uses them: its cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water, so water enters by endosmosis down the potential gradient. Plasmolysis and deplasmolysis demonstrate what happens when that gradient is reversed, and root pressure explains the slow upward push behind the ascent of sap in short plants.

facts.label: Root hair
facts.value: Single-celled extension increasing surface area; cell sap more concentrated than soil water

facts.label: Water pathway
facts.value: Soil -> root hair -> cortex -> endodermis -> xylem (cell wall route and cytoplasmic route)

facts.label: Key processes
facts.value: Imbibition, diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis, root pressure

blocks.text: Imbibition is the adsorption of water by a solid — swelling wood pushes aside stone, dry seeds swell and crack their coats, and cotton swells without dissolving. It requires a material with an affinity for water and a steep concentration gradient of the imbibed liquid. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration until uniformity is reached; it is faster at higher temperatures and greater steeper gradients, and in gases it is extremely rapid. Osmosis is the special case that governs plant water relations: the diffusion of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from the region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to the region of lower water potential (concentrated solution). In the laboratory, water moves from the distilled-water tube into the salt solution across a parchment membrane — the classic osmosis demonstration.

items.meaning: Adsorption of water by hydrophilic solids causing swelling, e.g. wood, seeds.
Net movement of particles down a concentration gradient until uniform mixing.
Diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution.
Permits water but not dissolved solute molecules — the property of living membranes.
Tendency of water to move; pure water has the highest potential, solutes lower it.
Water entering a cell / leaving a cell by osmosis.

items: Osmosis needs a selectively permeable membrane, a difference in concentration, and no energy input — it is passive.
Water moves to the hypertonic side (lower water potential); the hypotonic side is dilute.
Imbibition explains seed swelling and the pressure wood can exert.
Diffusion rate increases with temperature and steeper concentration gradients.
Osmosis is the process specifically responsible for water entering the root hair.

items.text: Raisins swell in water and shrink in salt solution — endosmosis and exosmosis.
items.note: Same dried tissue, opposite outcome, depending on which side is more concentrated.

items.text: Chips of dry wood jammed in a rock crack split it as they imbibe water.
items.note: Imbibition pressure can be enormous — a purely physical effect, no membrane required.

learn.title: How the root hair absorbs water

blocks.text: A root hair is a thin-walled, single-celled outgrowth of an epidermal cell whose large vacuole holds cell sap — a concentrated solution of salts and sugars. Because the cell sap is more concentrated than the surrounding soil water, water enters the root hair by endosmosis. From there it crosses the cortex, either travelling along the cell walls and intercellular spaces (the fast apoplastic route) or passing from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata (the symplastic route), until it reaches the endodermis. The Casparian strip in the endodermal walls blocks the wall route, forcing all water through the selectively permeable endodermal membranes into the xylem — the plant's checkpoint for what enters its transport system.

items: Root hairs increase surface area enormously — thousands per inch of root.
Absorption is by osmosis because cell sap concentration exceeds soil-water concentration.
Water moves through the cortex along walls (apoplast) or through cytoplasm (symplast).
The Casparian strip of suberin blocks the apoplastic route at the endodermis, forcing membrane passage.
Beyond the endodermis, water enters the xylem and is carried upward.
Minerals enter mostly by active transport using ATP — against the concentration gradient, unlike water.

items.text: Plant in hypertonic (fertiliser too strong) soil: root hairs lose water by exosmosis and the plant wilts — 'fertiliser burn'.
items.note: The soil solution became more concentrated than the cell sap, reversing the gradient.

items.text: Plasmolysed cells placed in pure water recover within minutes — deplasmolysis.
items.note: Recovery demonstrates that the membrane remained selectively permeable throughout.

items.meaning: Concentrated solution of salts and sugars stored in the root hair vacuole.
Suberin band in endodermal cell walls blocking the apoplastic route.
Continuous cell-wall pathway / continuous cytoplasmic pathway through plasmodesmata.
Positive pressure built up in the xylem by ion pumping, pushing sap upward.

blocks.text: When a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, water leaves the vacuole by exosmosis. The protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the cell wall — plasmolysis. The cell is flaccid, and a fully plasmolysed cell is beyond recovery if the exposure continues. Plasmolysis is reversible: transferring the cell to pure water lets water re-enter by endosmosis, the vacuole swells and the protoplast presses back against the wall — deplasmolysis. Wilting is the macroscopic consequence of plasmolysis in leaf cells: the cells lose turgor, the leaves droop, and recovery follows once water uptake exceeds loss. Turgid cells, meanwhile, provide the mechanical support that herbaceous plants rely on in place of wood.

items: Plasmolysis: hypertonic outside -> water leaves -> protoplast shrinks from wall.
Deplasmolysis: pure water outside -> water enters -> protoplast swells back.
Turgid cells give soft plants their support; loss of turgor causes wilting.
Plasmolysis kills cells if prolonged because the enzymes and membranes are damaged.
Osmosis explains both directions — the gradient, not the membrane, decides the direction.

items.text: Egg placed in salt solution shrinks; returned to water it swells again.
items.note: The same membrane behaves identically in both directions — only the outside concentration changed.

items.text: Cut flowers kept in a hot room wilt; placing stems in water restores them overnight.
items.note: Recovery is deplasmolysis of leaf cells once water uptake resumes.

learn.title: Root pressure and the ascent of sap

blocks.text: After water reaches the xylem, the endodermis actively pumps mineral ions into the vessel, making the xylem sap more concentrated. Water follows osmotically and builds a positive hydrostatic pressure — root pressure — which can push sap a short distance up, most visibly as guttation droplets at leaf margins on moist nights and as bleeding from cut stumps. Root pressure is too weak to supply tall trees; the main pull comes from transpiration at the leaves, which creates a tension that draws a continuous water column upward through the xylem. Root pressure matters in short herbs and in the initial filling of the system, but the transpiration pull is the dominant mechanism in general.

items: Root pressure is osmotic in origin: ion pumping into the xylem draws water in behind it.
Evidence of root pressure: guttation drops and bleeding from cut stems.
It is a positive (pushing) force and works best in small plants with short xylem paths.
Tall trees rely on the transpiration pull — a negative tension from evaporating leaves.
The cohesion of water molecules keeps the xylem column continuous under tension.

items.text: Grass blades exude droplets at dawn — guttation driven by root pressure when transpiration is low.
items.note: Guttation fluid is xylem sap with dissolved minerals, not condensed dew.

items.text: Stump of a felled tree bleeds for hours — the residual root pressure pushes xylem sap out.
items.note: A direct demonstration that the push comes from below, not from the leaves.

keyPoints: Imbibition: adsorption of water by solids; causes swelling of seeds and wood.
Diffusion: net movement down a concentration gradient until uniform.
Osmosis: water diffusion through a selectively permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated side.
Root hairs absorb soil water by endosmosis because cell sap is more concentrated.
Water crosses the cortex by apoplast and symplast routes; the Casparian strip forces membrane passage at the endodermis.
Plasmolysis occurs in hypertonic surroundings; deplasmolysis in pure water; wilting is field plasmolysis.
Root pressure is the positive push from ion pumping into the xylem; guttation and bleeding are its evidence.
Root pressure alone cannot lift water in tall trees — transpiration pull is the main mechanism.
examFocus: Osmosis answers must name the selectively permeable membrane and both concentration sides — direction alone is not enough.
Explain plasmolysis step by step: hypertonic outside, exosmosis, protoplast shrinkage, wall separation.
The Casparian strip is a favourite: state that it blocks the apoplastic route and forces selective passage.
Root pressure versus transpiration pull: give the evidence for each (guttation/bleeding versus tall trees).

vocabulary.meaning: Water movement through a selectively permeable membrane down water potential.
Water entering a cell by osmosis.
Shrinkage of the protoplast from the cell wall in hypertonic solution.
Pressure of the protoplast against the wall in a turgid cell.
Suberin band forcing water through endodermal membranes.
Positive hydrostatic pressure in the xylem produced by ion pumping.

questions.prompt: Water enters the root hair cell by:
questions.explanation: Cell sap is more concentrated than soil water, so water moves in across the selectively permeable membrane — the definition of endosmosis.
questions.commonMistake: Saying active transport — minerals are actively absorbed; water follows its potential gradient passively.

questions.prompt: Plasmolysis occurs when a cell is placed in a solution that is:
questions.explanation: A hypertonic (more concentrated) outside solution draws water out by exosmosis, so the protoplast shrinks away from the wall.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing hypotonic — that causes swelling and turgor, the opposite condition.

questions.prompt: The Casparian strip is important because it:
options: Forces all water through the selectively permeable endodermal membranes
questions.answer: Forces all water through the selectively permeable endodermal membranes
questions.explanation: The suberin strip blocks the cell-wall (apoplastic) pathway, so water must cross a membrane where the plant can regulate what passes.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking it stops water completely — it redirects the route, it does not seal it.

questions.prompt: Which is evidence of root pressure?
questions.explanation: Root pressure pushes xylem sap outward through hydathodes when transpiration is low, producing guttation drops; bleeding from cut stumps is similar evidence.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing transpiration — that demonstrates the pull from above, not the push from below.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the swelling of dry seeds when placed in water is an example of ________, which requires no membrane and involves ________ by a solid.
questions.explanation: Imbibition is water uptake by hydrophilic solids — cellulose and proteins in the seed coat adsorb water and swell.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it osmosis — no selectively permeable membrane is involved.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: water moves across the cortex by two routes — along the cell walls (________) and through the cytoplasm via plasmodesmata (________).
questions.explanation: Both routes operate until the Casparian strip, which blocks the apoplastic path at the endodermis.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the terms — 'apo' (away, wall) versus 'sym' (together, shared cytoplasm).

questions.prompt: Define osmosis and describe an experiment to demonstrate it in the laboratory.
questions.answer: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution). Demonstration: take a thistle funnel filled with sugar solution and invert it into a beaker of distilled water, sealing the mouth with parchment paper (a selectively permeable membrane). Water enters the funnel by osmosis, and the liquid level in the stem rises above the beaker's level; setting up a control with pure water in the funnel shows no rise, proving the movement is driven by the concentration difference.
questions.explanation: The answer needs the definition with direction, the apparatus, and a control to show the rise is osmotic rather than hydrostatic.
questions.commonMistake: Omitting the control or the direction of movement — both are regular marking points.

questions.prompt: Explain why a plant wilts when over-fertilised, and state what happens when it is watered generously afterwards.
questions.answer: Over-fertilising makes the soil solution more concentrated than the cell sap of the root hairs. The gradient reverses, so water leaves the root cells by exosmosis and the cells become plasmolysed and flaccid; the leaves lose turgor and droop — wilting. Watering generously dilutes the soil solution so that it becomes more dilute than the cell sap; water then re-enters the root hairs by endosmosis, the cells deplasmolysed and regain turgor, and the plant recovers if the exposure was not prolonged.
questions.explanation: Both halves follow the same principle with the gradient reversed — the answer must show why the direction of water movement changed.
questions.commonMistake: Describing wilting as 'over-watering' — the cause is the external concentration, not the quantity of water.

questions.prompt: Trace the path of water from the soil to the xylem vessel, naming each tissue crossed and explaining the role of the Casparian strip.
questions.answer: Water is first absorbed by the root hair from the soil solution by endosmosis, because the cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water. It then crosses several layers of cortex parenchyma, either along the cell walls and intercellular spaces (apoplastic route) or from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata (symplastic route). At the endodermis, the Casparian strip — a band of suberin impermeable to water in the cell walls — blocks the apoplastic route, so all water must pass through the selectively permeable membranes of the endodermal cells. Having crossed the membranes, water enters the pericycle and then the xylem vessels, from where it is carried upward through the plant.
questions.explanation: The trail is tested tissue by tissue; the strip's role is the pivot — it converts free wall flow into regulated membrane passage.
questions.commonMistake: Skipping the cortex or claiming the strip stops water — it forces membrane crossing, which is regulation, not blocking.

questions.prompt: Root pressure is often called 'too weak' to explain water movement in trees. Evaluate this statement.
questions.answer: Root pressure is a positive osmotic pressure of at most about one atmosphere (a few hundred kilopascals), sufficient to push water a few metres — adequate for short herbs, as shown by guttation and stump bleeding. Trees of 50 metres or more require a far greater force, and the water column under tension from transpiration pull can sustain hundreds of kilopascals of negative pressure (suction) with cohesion keeping the column unbroken. Root pressure is therefore real and useful at small scale, but insufficient for tall trees, where the transpiration-cohesion-tension mechanism dominates.
questions.explanation: The evaluation must accept that root pressure exists and does push, then quantify why it cannot scale to tall trees.
questions.commonMistake: Dismissing root pressure entirely — it works, just not at height; full credit needs both halves.
